transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-12-23
Start: 15:30 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes (scheduled)
Attendees: Eleanor Park (Redwood AE), Marcus Li (Redwood SE), Kai Gomez (Redwood CSM shadow), Priya Shah (Signet Eng Manager), Liam O'Connor (Signet Platform), Nina Park (Signet Security), Samuel Ortiz (Backend)
Shared: https://redwood.app/docs/sdk-quickstart , https://redwood.app/console-demo , internal: repo: github.com/redwood/quickstarts/signet (will share)

[00:00] Eleanor Park: Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. Quick intros — I'm Eleanor, AE on the Signet account, Marcus is our SE and he'll lead the code pairing, Kai's just joining to follow the onboarding. Priya, wanna kick us off with what you're most worried about?

[00:15] Priya Shah: Yeah hi thanks, so main things are making sure auth and keys fit our audit, and we want to get a dev fast path — Python first then TS. Also curious about console flows and what "Private" means for our VPC constraints.

[00:30] Marcus Li: Great, that's exactly what we planned to cover. We'll walk the SDK quickstart, show the console, and then go into an env setup for a sandbox vs a private VPC onprem-ish setup. We'll also point out Optimize suggestions for batching/caching.

[00:45] Liam O'Connor: Quick note — our infra team will want to see KMS integration and egress rules, we use GCP Workload Identity for service accounts.

[01:05] Marcus Li: Perfect, we have a short example for Workload Identity — there's a snippet in the Signet repo I'll share, it shows how to mint short-lived creds and exchange for Redwood tokens. It's under examples/auth/gcp-wi.md (we'll post link).

[02:10] Eleanor Park: Ok let's jump into code. Marcus, you can share screen for the Python quickstart?

[02:30] [screen share start] Marcus Li: Alright so this is pip install redwood-sdk (note: transcribed pip package may appear as redwood-client in some logs), then set REDWOOD_API_KEY or use the cli 'redwood auth login' which integrates SSO. We'll run a tiny generate example.

[03:05] Samuel Ortiz: Is there a recommended pattern to store keys in CI? We rotate using HashiVault.

[03:20] Marcus Li: Yes, we recommend using Vault/HSM/KMS and then inject at runtime. For CI, store a short-lived token and rotate — avoid embedding long-lived API keys in repo. We also support a client credential flow if you prefer OIDC.

[04:00] [00:04] Speaker 2: (mumble) can you repeat the creds exchange part?

[04:10] Marcus Li: Sure — one pattern: your workload identity binds to a small service account, you call the Redwood token endpoint with signed JWT, Redwood validates and mints a scoped token. For audits we include token introspection endpoints and full request logs in the console.

[05:00] Nina Park: For logs, does Redwood's console keep PII? We need to confirm retention and redaction policy.

[05:20] Eleanor Park: Short answer — you can configure retention and redaction. For Private deployments you can opt out of sending full payloads to Redwood hosted logs; we also provide audit export to your S3/GCS. I'll attach the SOC2/security pack after the call.

[05:45] Priya Shah: Awesome. Marcus, can you run the quickstart?

[06:00] Marcus Li: Yep. So example code:
from redwood import RedwoodClient
client = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY'))
print(client.generate("Summarize sales notes"))

[06:40] Marcus Li: Running now... you might see a small warning about kernel selection — that's from the local runtime shim if you're using the offload bin. Ignore for hosted.

[07:10] [07:10] Priya Shah: (laughs) that warning popped for us during internal test, thought it was a bug.

[07:25] Marcus Li: Common. It only shows up when the client attempts an optional quant path locally, we won't hit that on hosted.

[08:00] Marcus Li: Ok output looks good — next, TypeScript quickstart is similar: npm install @redwoodai/sdk (package name may differ in sample); import Redwood from '@redwoodai/sdk' etc. We demo both to make sure your frontend folks can onboard.

[09:10] Samuel Ortiz: For TS, we plan to call from a serverless backend — anything we should watch for re: cold-starts and token refresh?

[09:30] Marcus Li: Token refreshes are cheap, but avoid fetching a new token per request — cache per instance or use token exchange. For cold starts, prewarm or set a moderate cache TTL. We also have a small middleware example for express/next in the repo.

[10:10] Eleanor Park: Now let's open the Console. I'll show projects, API keys, and the Optimize tab.

[10:30] [screen share: Console] Eleanor Park: Here is the new Signet project UI (demo data). Keys -> create key -> can scope by route and model. You can set per-key quotas and IP restrictions.

[11:05] Nina Park: Do keys support RBAC and SCIM for user provisioning?

[11:20] Eleanor Park: Yes, SSO with SCIM provisioning + role-based permissions. For machine users you can create service roles and restrict scopes. We'll include the RBAC doc.

[12:00] Eleanor Park: Under Optimize, you'll see suggested batching configuration based on observed token distribution — e.g., increase batch size to 8 for mid-length prompts. That tends to lower per-token cost but monitor latency.

[12:35] Marcus Li: We also have KV/prefix caching for assistant contexts that reduces repeated KV hits for multi-turn. In some transcribes it shows as "K-V cache" and that sometimes comes out as "k v" in transcript.

[13:20] Liam O'Connor: Curious about quantization recommendations — we run mixed workloads, and cost is a major driver.

[13:40] Marcus Li: For workloads dominated by short replies, int8 or 4-bit quant will be great and cheap. For high-fidelity outputs or code generation we often recommend leaving a small subset of models unquantized or using quant-aware evals. The Optimize tab simulates cost/latency tradeoffs for a given prompt set.

[14:30] Priya Shah: Can Optimize run on our prompts privately? We don't want customer data in the simulation.

[14:45] Eleanor Park: Yes, for Private deployments Optimize can run locally against your sample prompts — results stay in your VPC. For hosted we do synthetic simulations or you can upload prompts with redaction.

[15:10] [15:10] Speaker 3: (background) is there a limits table for concurrent requests?

[15:20] Marcus Li: Concurrency depends on plan — Hosted has soft quotas, Dedicated gives guaranteed pool size and we tune pool per model. For Private you control capacity. We'll propose dedicated pool sizes in the pilot based on your SLA targets.

[16:00] Samuel Ortiz: About network egress — what ports and CIDR do we need to open for Redwood hosted?

[16:15] Eleanor Park: We'll send a simple egress table, typically HTTPS outbound to region endpoints and some optional peering ports for Private VPC peering. Liam earlier mentioned GCP WI — we'll give the peering checklist.

[17:00] Marcus Li: Ok let's do a short live codepair — Liam/Sam if you want to share your screen we can run the TS quickstart and debug auth.

[17:20] [17:20] Liam O'Connor: I'm screensharing now. Here is our repo, we copied the sample but get 401 on token exchange.

[17:40] Marcus Li: Hmm 401 usually means token audience mismatch or clock skew. Can you cat the JWT claims?

[18:05] Liam O'Connor: (typing) oh weird nbf is 10 minutes in the future... our CI runner clock skewed after DST update.

[18:25] Marcus Li: Yep that explains it. Quick fix: sync time or set small leeway in validation. We'll note that in the repo readme.

[19:10] Priya Shah: Great catch. Anything else to watch for in env setup?

[19:30] Marcus Li: A few gotchas — 1) CI should use short-lived tokens not hard-coded keys, 2) set per-route quotas, 3) tune batching otherwise latency tails can grow, 4) ensure your KMS policies allow token minting if using exchange.

[20:00] Eleanor Park: We'll now show the small bench script Marcus mentioned. It runs repeated requests and records p50/p95 and cost per 1k tokens.

[20:25] Marcus Li: Running bench now against a hosted dev model (demo) — here's sample output: p50 120ms, p95 320ms, cost $0.02 per 1k tokens. In your infra the network egress and VPC peering add a small delta.

[21:10] Samuel Ortiz: Those numbers look promising. How much variance do you see for multi-tenant pools?

[21:30] Marcus Li: For hosted multi-tenant you'll see slightly higher tail. Dedicated pools reduce variance and we can reserve capacity for burst windows. We'll include a few charts.

[22:00] Nina Park: About compliance — can we run this on-prem? We have air-gapped requirements for a subset of workloads.

[22:20] Eleanor Park: Yes, Redwood Private has an on-prem package and the private control plane option. We'll share the deployment diagram and an options matrix (air-gap, VPC peering, KMS via HSM).

[23:05] Priya Shah: Ok let's capture next steps and owners.

[23:20] Eleanor Park: Recap — Redwood to share: Signet quickstart repo, RBAC doc, egress checklist, SOC2 pack, bench script; Signet to run quickstarts and share any auth/logs errors; schedule pilot bench week of Jan 5th.

[24:00] [24:00] Speaker 1: thanks

[24:10] Marcus Li: A couple of micro-notes — when you run the bench use the sample promptset in examples/prompts/signet_prompts.txt, and turn on prefix cache to measure realistic multi-turn savings.

[25:00] Liam O'Connor: Will do. Also, about pricing can you send a simple estimate for 10k req/day given our profile?

[25:20] Eleanor Park: Yes we'll send a starter estimate and a dedicated sizing doc. Pricing will show cost delta for quantized vs unquantized.

[26:10] Priya Shah: One more question — our legal team asked about data residency in EU, we have customers in EU.

[26:30] Eleanor Park: We have region controls and can deploy Private in your EU region or host the project in the EU region to meet residency requirements. We'll flag the options in the deck we send.

[27:00] Samuel Ortiz: Slight tangential — do you have an example of fallback policies for when a model spikes? We want graceful degradation.

[27:20] Marcus Li: Yes, canary rollouts and fallback routing are built in — you can route to cheaper model variant when latency SLOs breach, and the console shows fallback rates. We'll include the routing policy examples.

[28:00] Priya Shah: This has been really helpful, thanks. Any security red flags we should know before the pilot?

[28:20] Nina Park: (interjection) I wanted to add that we'll need encryption in transit and at rest with keys managed by our HSM.

[28:35] Marcus Li: That's supported — we integrate with cloud KMS and HSMs for Private. For hosted we support customer-managed keys via KMS/HSM integrations and envelope encryption.

[29:10] Eleanor Park: Ok, final logistics: we'll share the quickstart repo and a conda/npm snippet for both languages, plus a short runbook for token exchange.

[29:40] Marcus Li: I'll also attach the bench script and a sample results CSV; it's tiny and should run in under 30 minutes for a smoke test.

[30:10] Priya Shah: Great. Before we close, can we agree on the pilot success criteria?

[30:25] Eleanor Park: Let's propose 3 success criteria: 1) Authentication flow works in Signet sandbox (no 401s) 2) Latency p95 below 400ms for typical prompts 3) Cost estimate within target threshold (we'll align on amount). Does that work?

[30:50] Priya Shah: Yes that seems sensible.

[31:10] Liam O'Connor: One last note — for the bench, include CPU/GPU metrics so we can map to our infra.

[31:30] Marcus Li: Will do; bench includes system metrics export.

[32:00] [32:00] Eleanor Park: Any final questions?

[32:12] Priya Shah: None from me, thanks.

[32:20] Nina Park: Nothing more. Thanks all.

[32:30] Eleanor Park: Cool. We'll send notes and the repo, and follow up on scheduling a pilot. Thanks everyone.

[48:00] [call end]

Notes about transcript: occasional speaker labels are generic (Speaker 1/2/3) where the recorder couldn't map; minor transcription errors present (e.g., package names and kernel warnings). Links and artifacts promised will be attached to the CRM activity.
